The house in committee on Bill No. 296, for the relief of Charles Edwin AValker- Mr. Sanderson-Mr. Power in the chair.
On section 1-Marriage dissolved.

This is a bill to
which the attention of the private bills committee should be especially called. The respondent denies that she is guilty. There are several corespondents named in this case. As I understand it, at the present time the respondent is in receipt of a separation allowance. She believes that this is simply a " frame-up" in order to relieve her husband of the responsibility of paying this separation allowance. In this case, as in a number of others, there is no notification given to the respondent before she comes to the divorce committee of the Senate as to what charges she is to meet. When she appears before the committee charges are introduced of which she has no knowledge whatever, and hence she is not able to produce witnesses in refutation of those charges. Further, only a limited amount of money is granted to her in order that she may make good her defence, and this allowance is not sufficient for her to call the witnesses necessary when several corespondents are named. I call these allegations to the attention of the private bills committee in order that this particular bill may receive careful consideration there. If not, I am afraid we shall have to take it up in detail and ask for rhe evidence here on the floor of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I feel somewhat the same way as my hon. friend. When the charge of adultery is brought against a woman she should have full particulars and ample time to prepare her defence. When she goes before the divorce committee and swears positively that she has not committed that offence, I give great weight to her evidence, because my experience is that in civil cases a woman hesitates very much before she perjures herself. I think a great deal is to be said in favour of this bill being reheard

by the private bills committee, or at least being postponed for further consideration by this house.
Shall section 1 carry?
No.
Those in favour of section 1 will please say "aye."
Aye.
Those opposed will please say "nay."
Nay.

In my
opinion the "nays" have it.
(Mr. BOYS: Mr. Chairman, I should like to know whether anybody appeared on behalf of the respondent when the bill was before the private bills committee. I do not know what the proceedings were there; I have not the record before me. One would almost imagine that if the respondent denied Ihe charge, and asked for an opportunity of calling evidence to prove the falsity of the allegation by the petitioner, her request would have been granted. I do not know whether she asked for the opportunity or not, but there is one sure thing, if she asked for it, and it was refused, there was no reason in the world why she Should not have appeared before the private bills committee when they had the bill under consideration and given some indication of her evidence and asked permission to call witnesses. From my knowledge of the atmosphere in the private bills committee this session, had that been done I have no doubt full opportunity would have been given her. If no such request was made of the committee why now should we be asked to send the bill back? I certainly do not want to stand against any woman wrongly accused, but it does seem to me there should be some finality to these proceedings. I am in accord wdth what has been said that perhaps the opportunities given to the respondents in these cases are more or less insufficient. There is nothing in the petition except the allegation that a certain woman has committed a certain offence with a certain man on divers occasions. Perhaps that procedure should be amended. But that is not before us at the present time. The divorce committee dealt with this bill. I think we ought to be told whether the request that I have referred to was madte. If it was made and refused, why did not the respondent through her counsel, or through my hon. friend, if he is interested-as he has been in other cases

Procedure Respecting Divorce
and taken action and well taken it-appear before the private bills committee instead of waiting until we get to the last days of the session before raising this point? It does not seem to me to be fair to the other side-and there are two sides to this question. I think before we send this bill back to the private bills committee, somebody with knowledge of the situation should acquaint us with the proceedings before the divorce committee and before the private bills committee when the bill was under consideration there.
Mr. Chairman, personally I know nothing with regard to the evidence in this case. It is some two weeks ago since I had a letter from the respondent asking that something be done for her protection.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I think the time has come when>
some stand should be taken by this house as to what right any member has to introduce and place upon Hansard letters written to him privately by one of the parties to a divorce action, which letter could never be admitted before a committee of this house or any court of justice.
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor.
I am raising a point of order.
The member for Simeoe has the floor on a point of order. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will please sit down.

My point of order is that no member of this house has a right to quote from a private letter he received from one of the parties to a divorce suit, which letter would not be admitted before either the divorce committee or the private bills committee or any court of justice.

With all respelct to the judgment of the hon. member for Simeoe, I am inclined to think that his point of order is not well taken. In my view any member of this house has a right in debate to quote any document if he will produce it.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to have that ruling. But it may relieve the mind of the hon. member for Simeoe if I tell him that I had no idea of reading a letter. He complained that this matter ought to have been brought to the attention of the house at an earlier stage. I stated that several weeks ago I had a letter from the respondent urging that something be done in the case. Now-

No, that is not quotation; it is a reference.
You might as well read it as state what is in it.

Will the hon. gentleman let me have the floor for a moment? A few .minutes ago he complained that nothing had been done, and inferentially he suggested some of us should have done something. I say I had no personal knowledge of this case, but that one of the parties concerned had written to me simply because I had been taking a stand in a general way against these eases. She had written to me asking that something should be done. I had brought one or two cases before the house. In this case I did n.ot want to weary the house at the time by reading another letter into the records and making another appeal. I am not a member of the private bills committee;
I have to attend other committees oif the house and to do work outside of this divorce question. I take it for granted that the members of the private bills committee, including the hon. member from Simeoe, should have given some consideration to this case when it was before the committee, but apparently nothing was done.
Would you suggest that we should delay it without a request from the respondent?
I suggest that every bill which comes before the private bills committee should receive consideration.
I suggest that the hon. gentleman had better read this case and the other cases before he starts to object to what has been done.

I would remind the hon. member for Simeoe that the only two measures which have been held up in this house and have been referred back to the private bills committee have resulted in one being withdrawn and the other voted down. Out of 250 cases coming before this house, only two were carefully examined by the private bills committee and both of them were rejected. I do not suggest that this proves that if all of the 250 were so considered that they wouLd all be rejected, but I do say that it is a most remarkable thing that such a decision should. have resulted in regard to these two. When I, as a private member of the house, am appealed to to take such action as will delay a case of this sort, it seems to me that I have a perfect right to voice an



Procedure Respecting Divorce
objection to proceeding with the bill. This woman the respondent in this case, claims that the whole matter is a frameup, and so far as I am able to observe the procedure as carried on by the Senate committee, the way is wide open for a frameup. Here let me emphasize a point which I mentioned and which I think is worthy of the consideration of this house: the respondent was given no opportunity whatever to know what Charges were being made against her. Several corespondents were named, and it would require a very heavy expenditure of money for her to bring witnesses from a distance in order that her case might be established, and possibly the evidence against her refuted.

Did the respondent's counsel
before the divorce committee ask for an appeal?
Yes, I believe so.
Was the respondent represented by counsel?

Yes, but that did
not altogether meet her need, 'because she had not the money to bring the witnesses who were required.

My hon. friend knows that if
she requires money an allowance is made.

A certain allowance is made, but I would ask the hon. member how far S75 will go in paying fees of counsel and in bringing witnesses to testify to several distinct charges. Here is one fact I gather from the evidence; the most material witness for the respondent was not able to be present. It is a queer 'thing that we should damn a woman in this way simply because it does not meet the convenience of the Senate committee to postpone the case.
Is the evidence to which the hon. gentleman has just referred the evidence in this case?

I am quoting from:
The petition of Charles Edwin Walker for a bill of divorce from Eva Mary Leroy Walker: report of the committee on divorce, together with evidence received by the committee. Minutes of evidence, the Senate, Ottawa. April 22, 1929.
On page 9 I read:

I have before me a resolution from the Associated Boards of Trade of Central British Columbia with reference to telephone facilities in the northern part of central British Columbia extending from Terrace for about three hundred miles along the Canadian National line, embracing the whole of Ominica county as well as the Skeena. I think perhaps at this time it would be well to let the minister know the great needs of this part of Canada in regard to an up-to-date telephone system. The resolution, I propose to read, is very brief:
Whereas present telephone facilities throughout the central interior of British Columbia are most inadequate, and many settlements are without this means of communication altogether ;
And whereas this large district, which is increasing in commercial importance every year, has to depend on insufficient telegraph facilities, and a tri-weekly mail service;
And whereas telephone lines traversing important parts of this district not served by telephone would be of very great benefit to the various business interests established in the district, and to settlers:
Be it therefore resolved that this convention of the Associated Boards of Trade of Central British Columbia do ask that the Dominion government have a survey made of the situation herein related, with a view to the construction of telephone systems where required, at the earliest possible moment.

I hope this matter will receive the sympathetic consideration of the government.

It is the desire of the department to impress upon the people who go to tlie outlying districts of the country the fact that they will not be cut off from the more settled portions of Canada and that they will be provided with facilities for communication with their friends and business connections so far as it is reasonably possible to do so.

I would like to ask the minister a question with reference to the telegraph service from Vancouver north along the coast of the mainland. I believe the line runs as far as Pender Harbour, and I understand that the service given is not satisfactory in that the offices are closed on Sundays and holidays. In the summer time a great many people go to the seaside resorts up along the coast and when an accident happens or someone becomes ill on a Sunday or a holid&y there is no way in which a telegram can be sent. It seems to me that some arrangement could be made whereby messages would be accepted by the Canadian National Railways Telegraph Company for delivery in Vancouver on Sundays and holidays. The

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Senn
men who send the messages are available because t'he offices are generally located in their stores. I have endeavoured myseilf to send out messages on several occasions but have found that it was impossible to do so.

These lines are pretty
primitive, and a great many offices are located in the houses of the operators. These men are usually available but they cannot be expected to stay on the job all the time. There is only one operator at each office, and there are bound to be periods when he would be taking time off. However, the sugestion made by my hon. friend is worthy of consideration and I shall be very glad to look into it.
I am afraid I have not made myself clear to the minister. The trouble is not with the men who send the messages, but with the delivery of the messages in Vancouver.
The bon. member's objection is that the receiving end1 is not kept open.

Yes. I suggest that
it might be possible to make an arrangement with the Canadian National so that they would accept messages from along the coast and deliver them in Vancouver on Sundays and holidays. They could also send out messages where the operators could be reached.
No complaints have reached the department with reference to the particular matter the hon. member has mentioned. We have an arrangement with the Canadian National applying to certain places.
Carried.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from a dairy district, where practically every farmer is a dairy farmer, I am naturally interested in anything that concerns or affects the dairy industry. I have listened carefully while hon. gentlemen in this house have declared that the importation of butter at one cent per pound duty did not injuriously affect our dairy industry. As I have listened to them it- has seemed to me that they could not be in very close touch with the dairy industry, at least with those whom this importation of butter most vitally concerns, namely, the producers-the dairy farmers.
In a great agricultural country like Canada, where all governments in the past have sought to encourage and fester the dairy industry, a country which has gained a place as one of the leading dairy countries of the world, it does seem to me reasonable that we should at least be able to supply our own requirements.
I think I am voicing the opinion of thousands of those who are engaged in the dairy industry to-day when I say that had there been no importation of butter at one cent per pound duty, our butter production would have kept pace with the times, and we would not now be importing such large quantities of butter.
For years the dairy farmers of the district which I have the honour to represent were urged by the department of agriculture to engage in winter dairying. We were told by the dairy and cold storage branch that our prospects for increased prices for butter would be better could an all the year round supply be provided. Now, in a country like Canada an all the year round supply can be provided only by winter dairying. Up to within a few years ago winter dairying was on the increase in our district, but at the present time, with the exception of the production of sweet milk for our towns and cities, winter dairying is practically a dead issue.
Dairying in Canada made great progress from 1900 until 1926. What is the reason that it has not continued to forge ahead? Is the dairy farmer less patriotic than he was in 
1926? Is he less capable of producing to-day than he was a few years ago? Rather is the failure not due to the fact that a few years ago this government took away the slight advantage which the dairy farmer held in his home market, and forced him-notwithstanding the fact that he must stable his cattle from six to seven months in each and every year and give them extra care-forced him. I say, to take a price for his butter based upon the competitive cost of producing a pound of butter fat in a country where conditions as to climate and feed are very favourable.
I thmk, Mr. Speaker, that the dairy farmers of this country have a right to expect fair play. Fair play is all they ask. It is a significant fact that Canada is the only British dominion that permits the importation of butter at 1 cent per pound duty. Australia has a duty of 12 cents per pound; New Zealand, 7 cents; South Africa- had a- duty of 4 cents per pound, but in 1926 when Australia succeeded in shipping large quantities of butter into South Africa the duty was raised to 10 cents per pound to preserve the home market to the South African producer; the United States has a duty of 12 cents per pound, and if indication counts for anything now, that duty will soon be raised to 14 cents per pound; Argentine has a duty of 6.18 cents per pound; while in Canada, where dairying is carried on perhaps under even more difficult conditions than in any of the countries that I have named, this government has decided that the only protection the Canadian dairyman is worthy of is one cent per pound. Since that decision was made and became effective, in 1925, the farmers of the Antipodes have been capturing the butter market of Canada. The Australian treaty was made applicable on and after October 1, 1925, and at that time by order in council the 1 cent rate on imported butter was extended to New Zealand. It is true that Australia did grant certain concessions to Canada in return for the concessions that Canada granted to her; but as far as I am aware neither then nor since has New Zealand granted any concessions to Canada in return for the concessions that Canada granted to her.
Now, I should like the house to note for a moment the imports of butter from Australia and New Zealand for the fiscal years ending March 31, 1921, to March 31, 1925, or the

Some people will ask, what about the consumer? They will say that if it were not for this importation of butter at one cent a pound duty the consumer would have to pay more per pound for this product. I am not so sure of that. The most discouraging thing the Canadian dairy farmer has to face to-day is the fact that he is not secure in his own home market. The people in the towns and cities of the districts I have the honour to represent are not much concerned about a few cents a pound on butter. They believe that the greatest asset they can have is a prosperous farming community at their door. They believe that a prosperous farming community right at their door is of greater value to them than a prosperous farming community three thousand miles away. Similarly, the fanners of that district believe that towns and cities at their door, where workmen are busy making the tools and implements they require on their farms-and the farmers of Canada at large require-are of greater value to them than prosperous towns and cities in the United States or anywhere else in the world.
The foundation of the entire dairy industry is the production of milk and the success of any one branch of that industry is no indication of the success of the industry as a whole. A farmer, if he is geographically so situated, will perhaps send his milk to the cheese factory this year and next year to the creamery to be made into butter. That is a common occurrence throughout Ontario. 1 repeat, the success of any one branch is no Tummon.]
indication of the success of the industry taken as a whole; but the production of milk is the foundation or basis of the entire industry. Upon it all branches of the dairy industry are built. From 1910 to 1926 the dairy industry in Canada made great strides forward; but something seemed to have gone wrong in 1927. It is well to remember that the Australian treaty and the New Zealand order in council wrent into effect fifteen months prior to the beginning of the year 1927. Let us note what the total dairy production in Canada was for the two calendar years 1926 and 1927-that is, the total dairy production of Canada expressed in pounds of milk and covering milk made into butter, both dairy and creamery, home made and factory cheese, miscellaneous factory products, and milk consumed fresh or otherwise. I regret that the dairy statistics for the year 1928 are not yet available, but I will venture this opinion, that when they are available they will show a corresponding decrease in the basis of the entire dairy industry production of milk in comparison with 1927. Let us take the decrease of 347,098,000 pounds in the foundation of the dairy industry in 1927; at the usual average ratio of 3-5 pounds of butter fat to 100 pounds of milk, this would represent 12,148.429 pounds of butter fat. A pound of butter fat is equivalent to 1J pounds of butter. Thus the decrease in the milk production in Canada in 1927 compared to 1926 is equivalent to 14,378.115 pounds of butter. Now we have a rather interesting comparison. If we go back and look at the importations of butter into Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1928, which covers the milk producing periods of 1927, we find that the importations were 14,195,789 pounds. In other words, the shrinkage or decrease in the base or foundation of the entire industry in 1927 compared with 1926, expressed in pounds of butter, agrees with the amount of butter imported during the same period from the Antipodes, and most of which came from New Zealand. There could be no stronger evidence to show that the importation of butter at one cent a pound duty from the Antipodes is gradually driving the Canadian dairyman back. The two oldest branches of the dairy industry in

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Tummon
Canada are cheese production and butter production. The importation of butter into Canada at one cent per pound duty does not come directly into competition with such branches as sweet milk for cities, condensed milk, sweet cream for ice cream and sweet milk and cream for exportation into the United States. The New Zealanders cannot compete directly with these branches, But the importation of butter does directly compete with those dairymen who follow the two old natural branches, the production of cheese and the production of buttter. The dairy farmers who follow these two branches are for the most part geographically so situated that they must depend upon these two lines for a market for their milk, and often, if they are so situated, they may change from one branch to the other from season to season.
I think this is clearly demonstrated if we look at the figures for Ontario. In 1927 as compared with 1926 the production of milk decreased by 473,924,430 pounds, but notwithstanding there was an increase of 5,930,745 pounds in the production of butter. However, there was a decrease in the production of cheese of 23,257,067 pounds. There was a total decrease in the production of dairy and cieamery butter in Canada of 230,340 pounds as compared with 1926; that is a comparatively small reduction, but the reduction in factory and home made cheese amounted to 33,776,051 pounds. Here again, if you take the pounds of milk necessary to make this quantity of cheese in addition to the pounds of milk represented in the decreased production of butter, you will find that it agrees. Thus in the year commencing fifteen months after the New Zealand order in council came into effect, under a duty of one cent per pound we had an importation of butter amounting to 14,195,789 pounds, which is equal to a reduction of 347,098,000 pounds of milk, the production of which is the foundation of the dairy industry, and 'the effect of that importation was reflected in the decreased production in the two natural branches of the dairying industry, cheese and butter.
On page 9 of the pamphlet issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with dairy factories we find that during 1927 the total delivery of milk to cheese factories in Canada was 1,384,860,282 pounds, but the decrease in the production of milk in that year as compared with 1926 was almost equal to one-quarter the total amount of milk supplied to all cheese factories in Canada in 1927. The total amount of milk supplied1 to all cheese factories in Ontario in 1927 was 1,080,187,411 pounds, so the decrease in milk production in that year as compared 78594-201
with 1926 is equal to about one-third the entire cheese factory supply of milk in Ontario in 1927.
If we exclude Ontario and consider the other eight provinces, the decrease in the production of milk is greater by 42,425,128 pounds than all milk supplied to all cheese factories in those eight provinces in 1927. As the previous speaker (Mr. Senn) has said, there has been a great decrease in the number of dairy cattle in Canada; in 1927 that decrease amounted to 75,275 milking cows, as compared with 1926. It may be said that United States dairymen are coming to Canada and buying our cattle. Why should they not do so? They are protected and secure in their home market, and they can come to Canada for our cattle. Surely there is something wrong with the dairy industry of this country, and when any business begins to go back it is time to look for the cause and apply a remedy. The dairy farmers know something is wrong and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) knows something is wrong, or if he does not know I wonder what he meant when he spoke before the National Dairy Council at the King Edward hotel in Toronto last November, where he is reported to have said:
You know that for the last year or two Canada has been relying on the west for the production of butter, and the west has rallied to that reliance by increased production. As far as I can see there is no visible increase in eastern Canada, and the west has been eon-verted during the last decade and a half from an importing country to an exporting country in butter. But now there has been a cessation of that increase during the past two years. We will not inquire into the reasons for it.
Then there was laughter.
There may be many and just as you will look at it, right up in Saskatchewan people differ as to the cause of it.
Then there was great laughter.
I feel that is true, but common sense wrill suggest to both east and west that whatever the causes may be, few or many, they should be removed at the first opportunity, otherwise our production of butter and other products is going to decrease. The west was your best bid for the production of butter, but whatever the cause or causes-it may be due to our poor class of dairy cattle; in our hard times we may have been induced to sell off our best cattle-
Imagine a minister of this government talking about hard times during the past two years! If a member on this side of the house made that statement he would be accused immediately of talking blue ruin.
-with the result that production gradually went down-it may have been due to nonnutritions feed during the winter and bad falls, which sometimes come about, or it may be a combination of all these and some other things.

3168	COMMONS
Agricultural Conditiom-Mr. Robb
Then there was great laughter, but the minister continued:
I take this ground, with your admonitions right in my mind; and I think it should appeal eventually to all of us that whatever the disabilities and limitations of the west to better production may be they should be diplomatically, quickly and quietly removed, whatever they may be.
That is the attitude we on this side of the house are taking on this matter, that the handicaps or disadvantages under which the Canadian dairyman is labouring to-day should be quickly and quietly removed. As the previous speaker just said, this is not a question of empire trade, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) does not look upon it as such. Speaking in Woodstock on September 21, 1925, the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
There is one condition of that treaty which says that we are free to alter or to abrogate it altogether on six months' notice. I say to the farmers of Oxford that if the Australian treaty does any injury to your industry I will undertake to say on behalf of the government that I will give that six months' notice on short order.
I say this is not a matter of empire trade but a matter concerning the welfare of the dairy industry of Canada. That is why we bring. this question to the attention of the government, and in the words of the Minister of Agriculture we say that the handicaps under which the dairy industry is labouring should be diplomatically, quietly and quickly removed.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who brought up this question on the motion to go into supply made the broad statement that this government had done nothing to help the farmers of Canada. When he made that statement I recalled the opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1924 when we reduced the duty on agricultural implements, on dairy utensils and on machinery required for work in our orchards, and removed altogether the sales tax from agricultural implements and dairy utensils.
Beautiful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman opposite says "beautiful," but I can recall that he was one of those who kept the house in session day after day protesting against this reduction in the duty on agricultural implements and on dairy utensils which we were told would ruin these great industries.

That is the reason the
treaty was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The agricultural implement industry in Canada is in better shape to-day than it was when the reductions were made. If the statements presented by my hon. friends to-night had any foundation in fact we would be unanimous in a desire to find out what the trouble was and how a cure could be effected.
What does the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) say about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to the prices received for
the products, I intend to show that the dairy industry is in a better position to-day than it was prior to the introduction of the Australia-New Zealand agreement. I fail to understand the logic of my hon. friends opposite. They do not want to trade with the United States because that country is placing restrictions against our products.
That is not quite correct; we are not allowed to trade with the United States.

I will show my hon. friend
in a moment that we are allowed to trade with the United States.

trade with the British dominions because, they say, they believe in the proper method of trading-paying with their own products. The favourable balance of trade for the years 1924 to 1929 inclusive as between Canada and Australia and New Zealand amounted to over $130,000,000.
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That means that we had a favourable balance of trade of over $130,000,000 more than we bought from them.
Is that a good thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Do hon. members argue that the men employed in the factories of Canada; the men employed in the woods getting out lumber and canying it to the saw mills and to the paper mills; the men who are employed on the railways hauling to the seaboard; the men on the docks-do they say that those men and their families are not consuming our farm products? I submit that this condition has brought about a greater consumption of farm products in Canada.
My hon. friend made a comparison between the position of the Canadian farmer and that of the United States farmer, mentioning the greater advantages which the American farmer enjoys. My reading of the press within the

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Robb
last few months has convinced me that the United States farmer, the man who has been enjoying the high tariff protection which hon. gentlemen opposite are preaching, is in a very much worse position than the Canadian farmer.
He wants more protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He wants more protection,
but what he really needs is a lower cost of living. I will admit at once that the dairy farmers of Canada would be helped very materially by a lowering of the cost of the feed products required for their stock. I will admit at once that under our freight tariff arrangement we encourage the export of bran and shorts, rather than their consumption in Canada. The millers prefer to export bran and shorts, not only because of the favourable freight rate but because of certain restrictions which prevent the miller from putting the mill-run screenings in the bran and shorts for local consumption while he is permitted to include them in the materia] exported. It is much more profitable for the miller to export, and that is a matter which might be deserving of some consideration.
Next year.

I am ready to take the judgment of any dairyman throughout Canada whether he prefers competition from oleomargarine or competition from butter coming from anywhere, butter that he himself can buy for his own family. As long as he is getting from $2.10 to $2.40 per 100 pounds for his milk, he is not complaining.
I repeat that something must be done for the dairy industry of this country by way of adjustment so that they will be able to buy their feedstuffs a little cheaper. The two great factors on a dairy farm are, first, labour, [DOT]and, second, feedstuffs. There has been a scarcity of labour on the dairy farms. Feedstuffs are not only high in price but in some cases unobtainable and it seems to me it would become hon. gentlemen opposite better to try to remedy that condition than to place higher tariffs against butter that is required, not only in the cities, towns and villages, but by many of the farmers throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, I am not in the least surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is extremely urgent in his support of the order in council which was passed by the government and which enabled New Zealand1 to receive the benefits of the Australian treaty. The Australian treaty is the child of the Minister of Finance. His predecessors had (failed time and time again to draw Canada and Australia nearer together on the question of a commercial treaty. The Minister of Finance succeeded. Unquestionably he obtained benefits for Canada, and the dairy farmer of the Dominion paid for those benefits in golden butter. In the session of 1925, after a very considerable debate, parliament accepted the basis of the Australian treaty. No sooner had that session ended; no sooner had hon. members returned to their ridings, than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking at Woodstock in September, pointed out that there was a method whereby Canada could be safeguarded should damage result. Be pointed out that there was in the treaty a clause which would enable the government of Canada to give six months' notice

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Stirling
to the other contracting parties, under which notice it would !be possible, for Canada to draw back on the treaty. Five days later the government of Canada presented to New Zealand on a platter the terms of the Australian treaty. Whether or not it was reasonable for the Prime Minister to .make any reference whatever to New Zealand when he spoke in Woodstock on the 21st of September is a matter for conjecture, but the fact remains that whether or not the government of Canada at that date realized that New Zealand would be asking for those terms, Canada gave those terms to Neiw Zealand, and although questions have fairly often been asked in the house as to what Canada received in exchange from New Zealand, we are yet in ignorance that Canada received anything.
After that, the dairy interests of Canada approached the government on many occasions, pointing out the difficulties that the dairy farmer in this country was subjected to on account of the importations of butter from New Zealand and Australia. At first the serious matter was butter from Australia, but as Australia adopted a plan known as the Patterson scheme, which produced what one might call a fictitious price for export butter, it was open to Canada to apply her dumping duty. That was applied, and butter from Australia ceased to come in quantity. Australia, perhaps not unreasonably, regretted that Canada had adopted this method of dealing with her importations, but it was interesting to Canadians to be able to remind Australia that not very many months before, Australia herself had applied very much the same treatment to New Zealand butter entering Australia. The National Dairy Council in their annual meeting in February, 1928, drew the attention of the government to the fact that the butter coming in from New Zealand, increasing and ever increasing, was a serious menace to the dairy interests in Canada. Their delegation met the privy council. They went so far fourteen months ago as to ask the government to rescind that order in council as regards New Zealand, but the government-the Minister of Agriculture (.Mr. Motherwell) we must presume, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) who fathered this arrangement -were of the opinion that they were better informed than the dairy men of Canada, and no action was taken to assist them. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that we have got into this difficulty primarily for the reason that we are governed in this country by a government whose fiscal policy reminds one of Nebuchadnezzar's image; for were we to describe this ministry member by member one could hardly avoid remembering that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) prates of freer trade, that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has achieved immortality by his accurate reference to Canada's protectionist policy, that the Minister .of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) has seen the light, that he would infinitely prefer his principles to override his desire for power, that he is busy day by day and week in by week out endeavouring to lead his colleagues into the paths of protection. Then we have the Minister of Agriculture, who on his arrival in Ottawa was undoubtedly a free trader from Saskatchewan. He has received a higher education in Ottawa, and he realizes to-day that there is nothing so very evil in a protectionist policy. He is assisting the Minister of National Revenue to lead the composite cabinet which governs this country into paths of protection, but unfortunately the Minister of Agriculture has been suffering from insommia. On occasion, when, unable to sleep, he rolls over and discovers a lump in his bed which on examination proves to be a pound of New Zealand butter. He examines the wrapper on that pound of New Zealand butter and finds that it is a Canadian creamery wrapper, but unfortunately when he minutely examines it he fails to discover in the most. minute print the fact that the butter came from New Zealand. The Minister of Agriculture was present when the National Dairy Council met in convention in February of last year. They made their statements in his presence and they came back at him again and again endeavouring to enlist his sympathy. When his turn came to speak he spoke in these words:
Let me draw your attention to another difficulty since we are pointing out difficulties in connection with the Australian treaty. Our western people, as you know, are preferably low tariff peaple. The moment they begin to agitate for a raising of duty, even though it is only to get it back to where it was, they are put in the embarrassing position of being high tariff on butter but low tariff on farm implements. It is no joke to take this position. I suppose it can be done, but it requires explaining. So you will sympathize with us all. I am sure you feel it yourselves.
Who was it said that?

The hon. Minister of
Agriculture, addressing the annual convention of the National Dairy Council in 1928. That the National Dairy Council may have altered its stand to a certain extent is perhaps explainable; for I have not yet heard in this house a contradiction of the statement that I have made, somewhat in allegory, that New Zealand butter is being wrapped in Canadian

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Stirling
creamery wrappers and sold to the unsuspecting consumer as Canadian butter. Perhaps when the hon. minster speaks in reply, or on his estimates, he may give us some much wanted information on that subject.
Who is doing that?
I refer the hon. gentleman to the hon. Minister of Agriculture, who knows everything connected with dairy farming in Canada.
It is not the Canadian farmer who is doing it anyway.

I have not suggested for one moment that 'the Canadian farmer is doing any such thing, because if it is being done in Canada it is being done to the detriment of the Canadian farmer, and he knows it. I do not know whether this government will consider the question of giving us any assistance in this matter, but I do know that the dairy farmer in the west and in British Columbia, which is beyond the west, is most rapidly altering his position with regard to tariff questions. He realizes that mixed farming is in a different category from wheat farming. He realizes that if he is not permitted a fair chance of selling his butter in the domestic market he has got to go out of business. The fact that the hon. Minister of Finance should use as his stock argument to-day, as heretofore, that the dairy farmer in Canada is getting more for his butter, leaves me absolutely cold. The price that the dairy farmer gets for his butter makes, I think, very little difference when you remember this fact, that the milch cows in Canada are decreasing, that the calves, are being vealed, and that the hogs are not being raised in the same numbers that they were, while at the time the number of milch cows in New Zealand is increasing. If the Canadian dairy farmer were satisfied that he is getting better prices for his butter to-day, would he be selling his milch cows? Would he not rather be increasing the size of his herds, and would he not be endeavouring to keep the domestic market for his own use? Canada is ceasing to be an exporting country and is becoming year by year an importing country. Is that a safe position for our dairy industry?

If it be the case that protection would increase the dairy herds of Canada, why is it that the cattle population of the United States has decreased by something like 17,000,000 in the last fifteen years?
It is larger this year than it was last. Surety the hon. gentleman knows that.

I would suggest, in the first place, that I was not preaching protection at this moment as the panacea of this ill. I was pointing out that the government of this country four years ago put over a trade agreement wdth a sister dominion, to which I have no objection, but the government bought the benefits of that trade agreement at the expense of a certain industry in this country which our Dominion Department of Agriculture and the departments of agriculture in all the provinces in this country are doing their very best to build up, and the result of that trade agreement has been a millstone aroqnd the necks of the Canadian dairy farmers.

I cannot compel the hon.
member to answer my question, Mr. Speaker-
You certainty cannot.
Because it is not a correst question.

I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when I am through, as I shall be in a few seconds, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) should tell us his own solution for the difficulties which confront the dairy farmer to-day. It appears to me that this government, having gone into a trade agreement with a sister dominion, and having then presented the terms of that agreement to another sister dominion-with both of whom we should like to trade if it is to Canada's advantage-must find a solution for this matter. Whether it be that they must adapt the arrangements that they had in mind when they were negotiating this treaty is for them to decide; but on the decision that they make the dairy farmers of this country will decide whether or not they will support the administration.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few
words on this question, largely to express my sympathy with agriculture and its difficulties. Perhaps I take quite a different view from that held by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house who have given us their views. I think I mentioned some time ago that the condition of agriculture is one of the world's prpblems of to-day. It is not only in Canada, in the United States, in Great Britain or on the continent of Europe that the farmers are having difficulties; as I said before, the condition is world wide.
I believe that to-day the farmers of Canada are more prosperous than those of any other country on the face of the globe. I do not mean that our farmers are getting everything

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Forke
they ought to get or that they are in the best position they could possibly attain. At the same time I am perfectly satisfied with the truth of that statement. In Denmark I found the farmers working on ten acres of land and making a living, but they were working from daylight to dark and were living with a frugality and working under such hard conditions as none of our western farmers would submit to. Coming over to Great Britain, I found hundreds of thousands of acres of grass land that it would not pay the British farmers to cultivate, and those Danish farmers were cultivating their small patches of land and selling their bacon and dairy products in the city of London. That is one of the conundrums that my hon. friends opposite may be able to solve.
A good deal has been said about our people going to the United States. Does any one know of any Canadians leaving Canada to farm in the United States?
Yes.
Many from my county have gone over to the state of Maine. I can count them by the hundreds.
It may be so, but I am surprised.
You are always learning.

If hon. members on the other side are satisfied that Canadians in large numbers are leaving Canada to go over to the United States to farm I very much doubt it. I think you will find them in the larger cities working at other occupations. Hon. gentlemen opposite know perfectly well that there is no exodus of Canadians to the United States to take up farming.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mafiion) made a speech the other day about the large number of educated Canadians going to the United States. I once made a speech of the same kind in Montreal, and I was surprised next day to see in large headlines in the Montreal papers that the hon. member, for Brandon was against education! You see how things can be twisted. I did not notice that the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William were treated in the same way. It will surprise the house to know that every year 25 per cent of the graduates of Acadia university go to the United States.
Why do they go?
That is a question which perhaps some one may be able to answer.
It is easily answered: you are responsible.
Order.

But only 5 per cent of the
graduates of the university of Winnipeg go to the United States. Tell me the reason why? Tell me why the maritime provinces are importing their butter at the present time.
So is Ottawa.

These are economic conditions and cannot be explained by merely laughing at my statement. To-night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) mentioned oleomargarine. I well remember that exactly the same type of speech as hon. gentlemen opposite are making to-night was made in this house at the time-that the dairy business was being ruined by the importation of oleomargarine.

What about processed
butter?
Order.

My hon. friend was in
the house at that time and he heard all the speeches then made.
You voted for it too.

Are the farmers of the United States prosperous to-day? What is the trouble with them? They are being caught in the same vicious circle. As the price of their products rises, so also does the cost of production. Our farmers will find themselves in just the same vicious circle if they think they are going to be benefited by protection. But I am not going to discuss the fiscal issue. I simply rose for the purpose of expressing my sympathy with agriculture and with our farmers in the difficulties they have to meet. I feel perfectly certain that the imposition of a duty of 2 or 3 cents per pound on butter will not solve the problem in the satisfactory way expected. There is something very subtle in the word "protection". When the farmer or any other producer has difficulty in putting his product on the market, and the word "protection" comes to his ears, it has a subtle influence over him and he thinks that such a remedy would benefit him. I do not know of anything more plausible than the argument for protection, yet every economic authority in the world has stated time and time again that the whole theory of protection is wrong in substance and in fact.

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Forke
The other day I picked up a United States publication called Farm and City Life. From it I jotted down the following 'in connection with farm operations in the United States:
Farm population smallest in thirty years.
Nearly 5,000,000 left the farm in the last 20 years. Not entirely due to hard times.
93,500,000 in the cities to-day; 75,000,000 in 1920. One person on the farm; 3.4 in the city, compared with 2.4 nine years ago. Increased production tends to balance these conditions.
Probable that increase in consumers will over-balance increase in efficiency of production, and gain will be to the farmer.
Why are people leaving the farm? Is the farm population declining in resourcefulness and ability as well as in numbers? Replies were received from 2,745 farmers. Some said it was a poor business; they could not make ends meet. One fourth were leaving the farms from physical disability-retired farmers. One in 40 had saved money to live easier and to move where more advantages could be found,- to the town or city.
The drift of young men and women to the towns is as old as time. One half were better on the farm; the cost of living consumed wages.
Advantages of country life-health; close to nature: the spacious character and independence of country life.
Upon the whole the country loses in efficiency and ability by the drift from the farm.

May I ask the minister
a question? Is he in favour of continuing the present importation of butter from New Zealand?

I do not think it will make
any difference.
Are you in favour of continuing it?

I am not in favour of continuing or discontinuing it; I will leave trade to make its own balance.
Some bon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

I do not see just exactly
where the amusement comes in. I have listened to several speeches to-night, and listened respectfully, and I sympathize with the farmers in their difficulties. I should like to see them get the best prices possible, and if it is likely to improve the condition of the farming population by any change in economics I shall be only too glad to support such a change. But I am thoroughly convinced that putting a cent or two more on butter would not benefit the fanmer in the long run, because as we can see in Australia to-day the farmers ate caught in a vicious circle. The farming population in Australia at the present time is in a worse condition than the farmers of Canada, and the same is true of the farming popidation of the United States; and the reason is just that; they are working in a

vicious circle of high production costs which more than counterbalance any increase in production which they may have.
I hope to see the day when the farmers of this country will enjoy prosperity in an increasing measure. I am one of those who believe that no country will be great unless its roots are firmly planted in the soil, and I deplore the effect of present world conditions on agriculture-not Canadian conditions but world conditions. There is a tendency for agriculture to sink lower in the scale and I deeply deplore the fact. It would be disastrous to Canada if the farming population of this country ceased to be a healthy, robust yeomanry and sank to the level of a .peasantry. Our country will prosper just in proportion to the prosperity of the farming population. I wish to see industry prosper too, but unless agriculture prospers this country as a whole will not progress. I rose merely to voice my sympathy with the agricultural people. They are the people to whom I belong and whom I love.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	At the time it was introduced I
opposed the Australian treaty because 1 believed that agriculture was sacrificed-at least it was not considered-in order that markets might be found for certain manufacturing interests in Canada. I want to support the Conservative members who have spoken, although I am not sure that I can support their remedy. They have not proposed one, but they have only one remedy for everything so I presume it is the same one. But so far as I have followed their speeches I think they have told the truth in regard to the condition of agriculture; agriculture is not in a sound condition. As regards the figures which have been given with reference to dairying, I am not sure whether I should find them the same if I looked them up; one can get figures to prove almost anything one sets out to prove. I shall not, therefore. enter into a discussion of the figures. I want to say a word or two, however, about the subject generally.
I was opposed at the time, and am still opposed, to the idea of the Australian treaty for the reason that the basic principle of lhat treaty was that the manufacturing industry in Canada should be considered while agriculture was not. Let me point out to the members of the opposition that I was opposed to the attitude they took on reciprocity for just the same reason. In the defeat of reciprocity the people who worked towards that end were [DOT] thinking not of agriculture but of the manufacturing industry, and I think we can truth-

Agricultural Conditions-Miss Macphail
fully say that the policy of Canadian governments, regardless of whether the government at any time has been Liberal or Conservative in name, has been to put the good of the manufacturers and their allies first, and the good of the great and basic industry of agriculture last. To my mind that is putting the cart before the horse. We have had it that way for a long time, and that accounts for the condition in which we find agriculture to-day. Protection is only a part of the contributing cause; there are many other things involved in the question which I do not intend1 to go into at the present moment.
One hon. member who spoke-I do not know him and therefore I cannot name his constituency-said that the people of the Canadian cities were very much concerned about the Canadian farmer. I am sorry to disagree with him; I do not think that statement is true. Of course, I do not mean that the people of his city are not concerned; but they are far above the average in intelligence. I find that the city people to whom I talk- and I have talked with people of many cities -know very little about the condition oi agriculture, for they are of the opinion, generally speaking, that agriculture is in a flourishing condition. They judge that by the prices they pay-the retail prices. If the dairy industry in Ontario could work out a cooperative system such as the wheat producers have developed, it would in some measure help to improve conditions.
I want to say only one word more. Protection, so far as the farmer is concerned, is in my opinion a snare. It may be that here and there the farmer would gain something; but I am absolutely convinced that on the whole he would lose much more than he gained, because he would then put himself in the position where he could no longer fight the protection of, for instance, the manufacturers. He would have lost the ground on which until now he has stood. So that if one could get a cent or two more per dozen for eggs, or a cent or two more per pound for butter, so far as the ordinary farm in Canada is concerned, that would have mighty little to do with the margin left over at the end of the year-if the farmer was happy enough to have one. The prices the farmers pay for the goods they consume and the prices they get for all the goods they sell are the factors that contribute to the margin when the year's business is balanced. If the Canadian farmer wants to learn about protection, let him look a little more closely into the condition of agriculture in the United States. The hon. member for York-Sunbury, (Mr. Hanson), I believe, seriously suggested
that a great many farmers were going from Canada to the United States. I do not think he intends the house to believe that he really meant that statement.

I said that in the neighbouring state of Maine, which adjoins my constituency, 25 per cent of the farmers of Aroostook county, 25 per cent of the farmers of Washington county, 25 per cent of the farmers of Somerset county, were recruited from the counties of Charlotte, York and Carleton in New Brunswick. That is the statement I made, and I can prove it.
Fifty years ago.

No, within the past ten
years.

Then certainly the
farmers in the maritime provinces must be in a bad way.
They are, since this government came in.

Anyone who thinks that one government or another is so important as to affect the condition of a basic industry like agriculture has a very childish mind. I have known of some farmers who did leave Canada to go to the United States to farm but I have not known of one who bettered his condition by so doing; and some whom I have known intimately very much regretted the change. That is all I care to say. As to the condition of agriculture as described by Conservative members who have spoken, I fully agree. The Australian treaty did not consider the agricultural industry, with that I agree. But with the proposed remedy which, though unspoken, is to be inferred from their speeches, that protection will cure the farmers' ills, I do not agree.

It is very fitting and necessary that this house should spend some time considering the basic industry of Canada. I am sorry that the house could not have had some definite information that this matter was to have been brought before us at this time. Had that information been afforded us, we should now probably have available the material which we have collected during the years and which bears upon the subject before us. As it is, we are more or less compelled to speak on a moment's notice and to depend upon our memories for Whatever facts we may bring forward.
I should like at the outset to point out that I do not think we shall solve this problem by the kind of discussion we have heard to-night and which we will doubtless con-
31/0	COMMONS
Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Irvine
tinue to hear until the subject is disposed of. The element of party polities is ever present in all discussions on the floor of the house, and I presume none of us is absolutely free from that feeling in the discussion of whatever subject may be under consideration. No doubt each one is trying his best to secure some advantage for his own particular party or group. That is one of the phases of our present parliamentary system which we must grin and bear. I do hope that in the very near future, however, the government will take the necessary steps to institute a thorough inquiry into the entire agricultural industry, an inquiry which will be quite untainted with partisanship and which will be conducted with a view to obtaining the facts as to the actual economic condition of the farmer and the general outlook of the industry and discovering what can be done to improve those conditions.
I am sure most of us will be grateful to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sena) who has brought this very important question to the attention of the house. No one will say that the agricultural industry of Canada is on a sound basis at present; in fact perhaps we must admit that agriculture does not seem to be on a very sound basis in any country. When all is said and done the agricultural problem of Canada is not peculiar to this country; there are agricultural problems of a very serious character everywhere, and perhaps one reason for this condition is that agriculture itself is passing through a phase of industrial development which perhaps we have not fully understood and to which we are not able quickly to accommodate ourselves. However, there are problems which are peculiarly Canadian, some of which might be mentioned in passing before I proceed to deal with the specific matter to which the attention of the house has been directed. I think agriculture is suffering, among other things, from .over-capitalization, with regard to the high prices paid for both land and machinery; and it is also over-capitalized because in relation to the amount produced the overhead is much too great. I would say also that agriculture is suffering from having to pay a much too high rate of interest. This is one of the chief hardships of agriculture in western Canada in particular. I believe that agriculture in Canada is suffering also from a decided discrimination in taxation. The dairy branch of agriculture has been affected by the Australian treaty; I do not think anyone can seriously deny that and it is . the dairy industry as affected by the Australian treaty which is before the house to-night.

I want to associate myself with the sentiments of the hon. gentleman who introduced this subject; indeed I must say that the dairymen of the riding of Wetaskiwin, which I have the honour to represent, have spoken emphatically on this issue. The Minister of Finance goes to the Montreal Gazette .to find out what the cows are doing, but he should go to the farmers of Canada to get that information,. I venture to say that -the minister will not go to the Montreal Gazette for the cream for his porridge to-morrow morning, and I do not see why he should go to that newspaper for his information as to the economic condition of the dairymen. At any rate, I know that the dairymen of my own riding have expressed themselves in no uncertain way to the extent that the Australian treaty has hurt their business, and that is the question now before us.
The hon. member who introduced this subject quoted figures to prove at least to his satisfaction a very material decrease in the production of butter and a further decrease in the number of dairy herds, with a corresponding increase in the production of butter and in the dairy herds of New Zealand. I do not know whether or not his figures are accurate, but I noticed that the Minister of Finance produced another set of figures. I think it is to be deplored that there seems to be no way of getting accurate figures. If we cannot get them right we would be far better off to leave them out entirely, but surely there is some source to which we may go for figures which may be accepted by both sides of the house. Apparently it is the practice for one side of the house to get the facts which suit them and for the other side to disregard those facts and secure quite different information. I am not charging that the hon. gentleman who introduced the subject gave incorrect figures, but it is very strange that the Minister of Finance should find it necessary to quote another set of figures practically the opposite of those given by the first speaker.
Personally I have no doubt that there has been a decrease in the dairy herds of Canada and in the production of butter, but as to the actual number of cattle or millions of pounds of butter I do not know. I would also agree with the minister that there has been an increase in the price of dairy cattle, but there has been a greater increase in the price of beef cattle which fact has affected the price of dairy cattle, so that certainly does not prove that the dairy industry has not been affected by the Australian treaty. I want to point out to the Minister of Finance and to the gov-

Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Irvine
eminent that discrimination has been shown against this branch of agriculture by the Australian treaty, a discrimination in the sense that the little protection which was given the farmers on the one or two items upon which a tariff is practicable was taken away and no corresponding reductions were made with regard to the articles which enter into the production of the commodities so dealt with. That is a discrimination. It has been said that the benefits to Canada of the Australian treaty were purchased and paid tor by the dairy industry. I do not think there is any doubt about that; if the dairymen are to be deprived of the protection which they had on the one or two articles on which it was possible to place a tariff, then they should have a corresponding reduction in tariffs on highly protected items which enter into their business.
It does not require any statement from me to prove that the farmers of Canada generally have expressed themselves as being opposed to tariffs, but I think I am correctly interpreting the opinion of the farmers of my own province when I say that they ask for equal treatment in this regard. If it is impossible to give them the same protection which is given to everyone else, then protection should not be given to anyone. That is their challenge. If you universalize protection, then no particular class will suffer. The nation may suffer or it may gain, as the case may be, depending on which is the correct view, but if you protect every class then no class will be unduly burdened. You must do one thing or the other; you must either protect the farmers equally with all other classes or you must not protect anyone. That is the position which the farmers in the west are beginning to take. They are opposed to tariffs, but they are saying also that they should receive equal treatment. If you are going to protect the manufacturers and then take off the protection which the farmers had, conditions will be a great deal worse. Protection is not a moral issue, it is a matter of dollars and cents. It concerns the implements and other things which the farmer needs, and no farmer can afford to set himself upon a moral pedestal and say: Because I have subscribed to a so-called Liberal doctrine for twenty years, that is no reason why I should allow my business to suffer from an injustice of this kind. This is not a moral question, it is an economic one, and economic principles alone must govern. In taking this new attitude the farmers of the west cannot be said to have abandoned their principles; they stand just as ready as ever for free trade.
Who authorized the hon. gentleman to speak for the farmers of western Canada?	.

The same ones who authorized the hon. minister to speak for them. I should like to ask the hon. minister who authorized him to speak for them. I am speaking directly for the greatest farmers' organization in the Dominion of Canada, and he was not.
You say so.

The hon. minister varied from the first principles of that organization, and discarded the principle upon which he was elected. If that is not a sufficient answer for the hon. minister I can give him more information, but I think that is all I need to say now.
Anything which the hon. member can say will not hurt; go ahead.
That comes well from a minister.

Perhaps if the hon. minister had a little more understanding it might hurt a little more; if he has not and it does not hurt, so much the better for him. I will challenge even the hon. gentleman who assumes to have the right to speak for all the farmers and say so far as I know there is no farmer organization in western Canada which has not expressed itself as being in favour of the principle of free trade, they are the only people however who do express those ideas. Nevertheless, they are saying: Since you will not give us free trade, do not protect everyone else and leave us to pay the bill. That is the position they are beginning to take, and surely ir is a reasonable one.
What does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) have to say in reply to this question which has been brought to the attention of parliament, this question which is engaging the serious attention of a very important branch of the agricultural industry in Canada? What remedy does the minister offer to parliament and to the people of Canada? His first point is to attempt to prove that the Conservatives had done even worse on one occasion. Mr. Speaker, I know that that is a very common political answer, and I do not suppose the minister is open to any more severe criticism for making it than is any other minister who has adopted that attitude in past years. I suggest to the minister that it is too much of an old-fashioned argument, it is too stupid an argument for a brilliant man like himself to present. I would ask him to drop that kind of parrying and face
3178	COMMONS
Agricultural Conditions-Mr. Irvine
the question squarely. What do the farmers of western Canada care about the allegation that on one occasion the Conservative party advocated the bringing in of oleomargarine and that such is said by the Minister to be much worse than what has been brought in by the Liberal party? That is no answer to the argument; it is not even recognizing the problem, and is unworthy of the minister.
Then the minister disputes the fact that there is a problem; he says it does not exist and that the removal of protection has increased the industry, given higher profits to the farmers, and, according to the Montreal Gazette, has produced more milk and more of thing else which goes to make a flourishing industry. Then another gentleman was appointed, and so on; I could go through page after page of this same sort of thing, but in spite of what is disclosed by this correspondence the minister tells me that the information given in reply to my question was correct. I say it was not correct, and it is for him to explain, in view of this correspondence, why he says that information was accurate.

I shall be very glad to
answer my hon. friend, to his entire satisfaction, I hope. I would say that there was considerable correspondence with my hon. friend himself. In looking over the correspondence I find that he has been fairly active in the county of Pictou. This was particularly true during the summer of 1926, when the party to which he belongs for a short time controlled matters in that and other ridings throughout the country. I would direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that when work is to be done in any particular county or constituency, naturally some local man is consulted with regard to the local situation. If a foreman is required, the engineer of this or of any other department could not be expected blindly to engage the man wdtfaout having him recommended by someone. That has not been the practice for a number of years in that riding or in any other riding. There is a great deal of difference between consulting a man as to whom he would recommend, and accepting that recomendation or continuing the man in service when he has proved to be unsatisfactory.
Or if his politics were bad.
When you are looking for a foreman, that question is not nearly so important as are his [DOT]qualifications for that particular job.
They were more important in the case of McLean; that has been abundantly proven.

When he was reported
upon as not being satisfactory he was promptly dismissed.
